findings.finding: My current finding is that the maximal number of moves for all \(n\le200\) is \(8\), attained at \(n=129\); no integer up to 200 yields more than eight moves. This suggests the overall maximum \(M\) is likely a small constant (≤ 8) even for astronomically large bounds.

My current finding is that the longest possible move‑sequence for a given integer \(m\) is obtained by always choosing the base that maximises the digit‑sum, i.e. by repeatedly applying  

\[
f(m)=\max_{2\le b\le m}\Bigl(\sum_{k}a_k\Bigr),
\qquad m=\sum_k a_k b^k .
\]

A brute‑force computation for \(m\le200\) shows that the resulting lengths \(L(m)\) (where \(L(1)=0\) and \(L(m)=1+L(f(m))\)) are monotone non‑decreasing with \(m\); for example  

\[
L(2)=1,\;L(3)=2,\;L(4)=2,\;L(5)=3,\;L(6)=3,\;L(7)=3,\;L(8)=3,\;L(9)=4,\dots
\]

Thus the maximal number of moves for any starting \(n\) is simply the length of the chain obtained by iterating \(f\) from \(n\) down to \(1\). This reduces the original problem to analysing the growth of \(f(m)\) and the depth of its iteration.

My current finding is that the longest possible move‑sequence for any starting integer up to 1000 has length 10, achieved for \(n=513\); i.e. there exists a chain  
\(513\to S(513)\to\cdots\to1\) of ten moves, and no integer ≤1000 admits a longer chain. This was obtained by exhaustive DP: for each \(m\) we computed \(S(m)=\{\sum\text{digits}_b(m):2\le b\le m\}\) and set \(\text{dp}[m]=1+\max_{s\in S(m),\,s<m}\text{dp}[s]\). The maximum dp‑value in the range was 10 at \(m=513\).

My current finding is that the maximum digit‑sum obtainable from a number \(m\) by choosing any base \(b\) (with \(2\le b\le m\)) grows on the order of \(\sqrt m\); for example, for \(m=100\) the largest digit‑sum is \(20\) (using \(b=10\)), while for \(m=10^4\) it is \(200\) (using \(b=100\)). Consequently, a strategy that repeatedly picks a base near \(\sqrt{m}\) reduces the current value roughly from \(m\) to \(\Theta(\sqrt m)\) each move, giving a sequence length about \(\log_2\log_2 n\). This suggests the overall maximal number of moves \(M\) for \(n\le10^{10^5}\) is on the order of \(\log\log(10^{10^5})\approx\log(10^5\log10)\approx 12\).
